Since a saying may be accepted because it is grounded in God, exalted is He, even if it is not in itself rational, He said: ﴿nor a Book﴾, that is, from God; and He described it by what is its necessary property that never separates from it, saying: ﴿illuminating﴾, that is, clear to the utmost clarity, making clear to others in the manner of God's clarifying, glory be to Him and exalted; or it is meant that the description is miraculousness, to manifest with certainty that it is from God, for not every Book of God is like that.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 31, verse 21:

Since the one who argues without any of these three (kinds of proof) is necessarily a follower of his own desire, imitating others like himself, and since the state of these disputants is strange given how evident the proofs of God's oneness are, He expressed amazement at them a second time, at their persistence in misguidance despite the clarity of the proofs, and said: ﴿And when it is said﴾, i.e., by whatever speaker it might be. Since the misguidance of a group is more astonishing than that of an individual, and since the amazement at the disputing of one person is an amazement at the disputing of two or more, a fortiori, He used the singular first and here used the plural, saying: ﴿to them﴾, i.e., to these disputants: ﴿Follow what﴾, i.e., exert your utmost effort in following that which ﴿God has sent down﴾, and He made it explicit, for added reproach, saying: ﴿God has sent down﴾, Who created you and created your first forefathers, and Who is the Mighty, and none is mighty but Him. ﴿They say﴾, (p-188) in stubbornness: We will not do that. ﴿Rather we will follow﴾, even if we strive with our souls and wealth, ﴿what we found our fathers upon﴾, because they are more firm in intellect, more upright in speech, and more rightly guided in way than us.

Since they do not travel a sensory path without a guide, the implied meaning is: Will you follow them, even if desire were calling them, in what you found them upon, toward that which is presumed to be destruction, because it lacks any proof? So He joined to it His saying: ﴿Even if Satan﴾, i.e., the one far from mercy, burning with the curse, who is their greatest enemy, were their guide, ﴿calling them﴾ to misguidance, thereby causing them to fall into what angers the Most Merciful, and that leads them ﴿to the punishment of the Blaze﴾. He expressed it in the present tense to depict their state in their misguidance and that it is continuous, and He used "the punishment" to refer to its cause.

Since the sense is: "Whoever disputes about God has no firm hold," He connected to it His words, describing the state of its opposites: ﴿And whoever submits﴾, that is, in the present or future state, ﴿his face﴾, that is, his intention, his orientation, and his whole self. Since the aim of the surah is to establish wisdom, He used the verb with "ila" (to) to alert to the soundness of the path through intermediaries, from the Prophet or the shaykh (spiritual guide), and guidance in this is excellent. He then said, linking it to what is implied, "covering and reaching": ﴿to God﴾, who possesses the attributes of perfection, (p-189) so that nothing of his own self remains at all. He does not move except by one of the commands of His glorified self. ﴿And He﴾, that is, while he ﴿is a doer of good﴾, that is, sincere inwardly as he is sincere outwardly, so he is always in a state of witnessing. ﴿Then he has grasped﴾, that is, he has produced the holding with the utmost strength he is capable of at the outset of affairs, to elevate his soul from its lowliness to the summit of the spirit at the hands of the wayfarers (al-musliquin, those who guide others along the spiritual path) whom He chose for His religion, who know the dangers of the journey and the obstacles of the way, ﴿by the firmest handhold﴾, which is the most secure thing to hold, so there is no falling for him at all. Let his gratitude therefore delight you, for his Lord will raise him to every desired goal as long as he holds fast to it. This is an illustration of the state of this traveler by the state of one who fell into a well, or who wished to climb a mountain, and his companion offered him a rope with loops, so he took hold of the most secure of them, and he rises with it when his friend pulls him. And He is certainly able [to pull him] without doubt, without its breaking, because his grasp is in the utmost firmness.

Since all are returning to Him and heading toward Him, those who hold to the most secure, those who hold to the weakest, and those who hold to nothing, except that the first returns in safety while the others return to ruin, He said, showing the greatness of the matter and so that it is not restricted by a circumstance, linking to what is implied: "So he arrives at God safe; to God is his end without doubt": ﴿And to God is the return of all affairs﴾, that is, to the Supreme King alone do they return, ﴿the outcome of affairs﴾, that is, just as their beginning was from Him. He specified the outcome only because they acknowledge the beginning.

(p-190) When He mentioned the Muslim, He mentioned the disbeliever, saying: ﴿And whoever disbelieves﴾, i.e., conceals what his intellect led him to, that Allah has no partner and that there is no power [at all] for anyone other than Him, and does not submit his face to Him. He became arrogant toward the callers (to faith) and refused to yield to them, following what his desire led him to, by making for himself a choice and an action resembling the act of the Strong, the Capable. Thus he has cast himself into every ruin, because he has not held fast to anything. ﴿So let not his disbelief grieve you﴾, i.e., let it not concern you or pain you. He used the singular pronoun in view of the word "whoever" (man), intending to specify each individual, and so said: ﴿his disbelief﴾, whoever he may be, for nothing of good has escaped you in him, and there is no incapacity on our part that would make you grieve, nor any responsibility upon you because of him. The use of the past tense here and the present tense in the first clause is good tidings that many will enter this religion and that they will not apostatize after their Islam, and an encouragement to Islam for everyone who is outside of it. So the verse is of the type of ihtibak (elliptical balancing): it mentions the grief second as evidence of the omission of its opposite first, and mentions holding fast first as evidence of the omission of its opposite second.

Since "grief" (al-huzn) has the meaning of concern (al-hamm), the causal explanation was made fitting by his words, turning to the locus of Majesty (mazhar al-'azamah), of which this is one of the most hidden aspects, and He used the plural because encompassing by the plural is more indicative of majesty: ﴿To Us﴾, i.e., exclusively, by virtue of the Majesty that belongs to Us, which mountains cannot withstand. ﴿Is their return﴾, i.e., their return, its time and its place, meaning in this world in sense and in the Day of Reckoning in actuality, not to other than Us. Since He made clear that they are in His grip and that their resurrection is necessary, He made clear that the cause of this is their reckoning, so that wisdom may appear, and so said: ﴿Then We will inform them﴾ by virtue of Our encompassing of their affair, and upon their return ﴿of what they did﴾, i.e., and We will recompense them for it if We wish.

Since the meaning of the intensive form (of nabba, "to inform") is: We shall deal with them as one who searches into matters and inquires into their evident and hidden aspects, their great and their minute, leaving none of them unexamined, He explained it by saying, expressing it with the Greatest Name, which conveys Majesty and other attributes of perfection, of which the greatest is knowledge, turning the speech away from Majesty, which indicates nothing else except by necessary implication, emphasizing against their denial the comprehensiveness of His knowledge: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Knowing﴾, i.e., encompassing in knowledge by virtue of His encompassing of the attributes of perfection ﴿of what is within the breasts﴾, i.e., of the deeds that are their companions, and what is latent and deposited within them, arising from them and before they emerge into existence; so how (much more so) with that after their doing.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 31, verse 24:

When the Muslim longed for the destruction of those of whom this is the state, and for knowledge of the duration of that, and haste being part of human nature, He answered the one who seeks to hasten (the punishment) with His words, returning to the manifestation of greatness, which calls for the humbling of the enemy and the honouring of the friend: ﴿We shall let them enjoy themselves a little﴾, [i.e.] of time and of worldly portions, even though that is great in the eyes of one who has no knowledge. So do not occupy yourselves with hastening (punishment) against them, for everything that is coming is near.

Since compelling the arrogant towards punishment is something deemed remote, He used the distant demonstrative particle to point to what occurs in that case of the attributes of majesty, which humble men and crush mountains. Within this there is also an indication of the prolonged state of the wrongdoers during their enjoyment, even if it is little in reality, or in the sight of God. So He said: ﴿Then We shall drive them﴾, i.e., We shall seize them with a seizure from which they cannot escape by any kind of stratagem. He indicated the lengthy humiliation of them over the period of driving by the particle of limit (ila, "to"), so the meaning is: then We shall, by that seizing, bring them ﴿to a harsh punishment﴾, i.e., severe and heavy, which will never cease from them at all, and they will find no escape from it from any of its directions. It is as though, in its severity and heaviness, it is a body extremely coarse, which, when it settles upon something, that thing cannot free itself from it.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 31, verse 25:

Since it is among the most wondrous of wonders that they dispute, despite their acknowledging what necessarily binds them to accept with certainty that He is the One, with no partner, and that He possesses all the attributes of perfection, so to Him belongs all praise, He said: ﴿And if﴾, i.e., they argue or say, "Rather, we follow our fathers," while the situation is that if ﴿you ask them: Who created the heavens﴾ in their entirety ﴿and the earth﴾ and all that is in them, ﴿they will surely say﴾. Since the most fitting thing for wisdom, which is the opening theme of the surah, is to restrict oneself to the place of need, he did not add here to the subject (al-musnad ilayhi), unlike in Surah al-Zukhruf, whose basis is clarification. So he said, turning the saying from the Majesty to what is greater than it, and said: ﴿Allah﴾ [i.e.] "the One named by this name, whose named one combines majesty and generosity." So they have acknowledged that everything they associated with Him is part of His creation and one of His made things.

Since they believed that their partners perform some actions for them, which is why they hoped in them and feared them, as is clear in the story of the uncle of Anas, the deaf, and others, he ﷺ was commanded to teach them that there is no creator other than Him and no command, but rather He is the originator of everything in the heavens and the earth, just as He originated them, and that among (p-194) the totality of that, by which He deserves praise, glory be to Him, is that He compelled them to believe in him (ﷺ) [by means of] this acknowledgment while they were at the extreme of denial. So he said, resuming: ﴿Say: All praise﴾, i.e., the encompassing of all attributes of perfection, ﴿is for Allah﴾, i.e., He to whom belongs the comprehensive, complete encompassing without restriction to the creation of the two worlds or anything else. "The matter is greater than the saying of any speaker." Just as He encompasses what you know of the creation of the heavens and the earth, so He is the doer of all actions, just as He is the creator of all essences, and He has no partner in any part of the command, just as He has no partner in any part of the creation.

Since they used to suppose that their idols produce something, as the woman of Dhu al-Nur al-Dawsi, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Is the little girl to be feared from Dhu al-Shara?", and as the people of Dimam ibn Tha'laba, may Allah be pleased with him, said when he reviled their gods: "Beware of leprosy, beware of white leprosy," and as the attendant of al-'Uzza said, and as Thaqif said about their tyrant, to the extent that when it was leveled to the ground they said, "By Allah, the foundation will surely be angered," until that moved al-Mughira ibn Shu'ba, may Allah be pleased with him, to dig up the foundation. And when adversity touched them, especially at sea, they would disown them and attribute the matter to the One to whom it belongs, as is the content of monotheism. So perhaps someone would say, relying on that: (p-195) "They truly know what the praising has established." He said: ﴿But most of them do not know﴾, i.e., that Allah is the one alone responsible for everything, just as He alone created the heavens and the earth, and that nothing occurs except by His permission, because they do not act upon what they know of that, and knowledge not acted upon is non-existence; rather, non-existence is better than it. The few were the moderate ones at the deliverance from hardship, as will come shortly. Or the meaning is that they have no knowledge at all, for had they had knowledge it would have benefited them in their knowledge of Allah, or in that they do not acknowledge His sole right, glory be to Him, to create and provide, so that would necessitate their contradiction and oblige them to acknowledge the truth of your ruling on His oneness absolutely.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 31, verse 26:

When He had established for Himself, glory be to Him, the encompassing of the attributes of perfection, He began to adduce proof for that, saying, making clear that what He has informed us is His creation belongs to Him: ﴿To Allah belongs﴾, that is, the Great King who encompasses all the attributes of perfection exclusively, to the exclusion of others, ﴿whatever is in the heavens﴾, all of them. And when it was established from what preceded that they know and acknowledge what necessarily follows from it, namely His oneness, He did not emphasize by repeating ﴿whatever﴾ and the preposition, but said ﴿and the earth﴾, that is, all of it, just as both were among what He created, so it is not valid that any part of that be a partner to Him.

And when this was established, it necessarily produced His saying ﴿Indeed Allah﴾, that is, the Great King, ﴿He is﴾, or He alone, and it was emphasized because their claim of a partner entails denying His self-sufficiency. For this reason He placed the explicit name in the position of the pronoun, indicating that everything described by it is established for Him absolutely, without restriction to a particular respect: ﴿the Self-Sufficient﴾ absolutely, because all things belong to Him and are in need of Him, while He has no need of anything at all. And since self-sufficiency may not necessarily entail praise of Allah, He said ﴿the Praiseworthy﴾, that is, the one deserving of all praises, because He is the Bestower of blessings in the absolute sense, praised by every tongue, the tongues of states and of words; and even if their utterance is blame, it is praise insofar as He is the One who made them speak, and from the restraint of muteness He released them.

The Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on Surah 31, Verse 27:

Since the Self-Sufficient (al-Ghani) may have wealth that is confined, as in the heavens and the earth, which he mentioned as belonging to Him, and the One Worthy of Praise (al-Mahmud) may have that for which He is praised restricted and bounded, He established that it is otherwise. Rather, there is no limit to His self-sufficiency, and no restriction on His known things and His capabilities, which necessitate His praise, and no end to them. So He said: ﴿And if﴾, meaning, He has the two attributes mentioned, while the condition is that if ﴿whatever is in the earth﴾, meaning all of it, and this indicates comprehensiveness (istighraq) and the tracing of every single member of the category, with His saying ﴿of a tree﴾, where He used the singular, ﴿were pens﴾, meaning, and the tree is supplied after it by seven more trees, by way of hyperbole, and that whatever is in the earth of sea is ink for those pens, ﴿and the sea﴾, meaning, and the condition is that the sea. According to the reading of the Basrans (al-Basriyyun) with the accusative, the estimated reading is: "And if the sea" ﴿is supplied by it﴾, meaning, it becomes a supply and an increase to it ﴿after it﴾, meaning (p-197) from behind it ﴿seven seas﴾. So it was written with those pens and that ink, of which the whole earth is an inkwell, ﴿the words of Allah﴾ ﴿would not be exhausted﴾. He repeated the Greatest Name (al-Ism al-A'zam) to magnify the station, and so He said, making it manifest to indicate, along with blessing, the non-restriction to anything, however great: ﴿the words of Allah﴾. The pens and the ink would be exhausted. By using the plural of paucity (jam' al-qilla) together with its annexation to the name of the Essence, He indicated an increase in greatness through the inability to [write] even that small amount. Thus the inability to [write] the words is understood a fortiori. The creative origination (al-ibda') follows the words, so there is no word except to bring about some matter of the matters.

﴿Indeed, His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [Ya-Sin: 82]. From this it is known that all the seas would be exhausted, because they are finite, so they cannot suffice for what is not finite. How great is a greatness that has no end! And a pride that cannot be matched or rivaled! Therefore, the result of that was His saying, emphasizing, because their claim of a partner is a denial of His might, and the denial of resurrection is a denial of His wisdom: ﴿Indeed, Allah﴾, meaning, the One who encompasses everything in power and knowledge, without any restriction at all, ﴿is Almighty﴾, meaning, He overpowers everything and nothing overpowers Him, ﴿All-Wise﴾, meaning, He perfects what He wills, so no one can undo it, and no one among His creation has knowledge except what He has taught him, and no one among them has wisdom except to the measure that it has been bestowed upon him. It is known that the verse is of the device of ihtibak (the interlocking of complementary elements): He mentioned the pens as evidence for the omission of their ink, and He mentioned the seven [in] the hyperbole of the seas as evidence for its omission in the trees. This is of the great arts of this discipline. It is also known from the context that what is meant by "seven" is hyperbole in abundance, not its literal number, and that what is meant by the plural of paucity in "seas" is abundance, due to the indicator of hyperbole, while the plural of paucity in "words" is its literal meaning, so that the meaning is coherent. All of this is permissible and common in the language of the Arabs.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (*Nazm al-Durar*) on surah 31, verse 28:

After concluding with these two attributes, following the affirmation of the power to originate creation without end, he mentioned some of their effects in the resurrection (al-ba'th), which had been mentioned at the beginning of the surah and throughout it, up to the warning to them about it in His saying, ﴿To Us is their return﴾. So He said: ﴿Your creation﴾, meaning all of you, in His might and wisdom, ﴿is only like the creation of a single soul﴾. He repeated the negation explicitly for each of creation and resurrection separately, so He said: ﴿Nor your resurrection﴾, meaning all of you, ﴿is only like that of a single soul﴾, meaning like the resurrection of one soul. He specified the singular to establish the meaning and to emphasize the ease, so He said: ﴿single﴾. For His words, although they are not exhausted, are executed, and His power, although it is everlasting, is far-reaching. Thus the relation of the few and the many to His power is on one and the same footing, because no affair preoccupies Him from another affair. Then He indicated this by His saying, emphasizing it, because their denial of His Messenger and their rejection of what He honored them with includes a denial that they could be within His sight (p-199) and hearing: ﴿Indeed, Allah﴾, that is, the Sovereign Most High, who possesses comprehensive encompassment, ﴿is Hearing﴾, that is, of far-reaching hearing, who hears everything that can be heard of meanings at one time, none of them preoccupying Him from another. ﴿Seeing﴾, of far-reaching sight, who likewise sees everything that can be seen of physical things and meanings. Whoever is like this, all-encompassing in knowledge, far-reaching, complete in all-encompassing power, sees all the parts of every dead thing and hears everything that is heard of its meanings. So by the encompassment of His knowledge and the comprehensiveness of His power, He gathers those parts, distinguishes some of them from others, and returns to them those meanings, and then they are immediately standing, as they were the first time, in less than the blink of an eye.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 31, verse 29:

Having established this astonishing sign, he indicated it through a matter perceived by the senses, which is witnessed every day twice, together with its indication of the subjugation of what is in the heavens and the earth, and the refutation of their saying: ﴿And nothing destroys us except time﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 24], by showing that it is He who brought into existence time through the motion of the celestial spheres. The address is specific to one who understands this properly, and no one else, or it is general to every intelligent person, as an indication that in its indication of resurrection it is in the utmost clarity. So He said: ﴿Do you not see﴾, that is, O you who are fit for such an address, and it is possible that it is for the Prophet ﷺ, because no one among the created beings knows this with true knowledge except Him.

Since resurrection is like the bringing into existence of each of the two alternating phenomena (night and day) after their annihilation, denying it amounts to denying this, so He drew attention to that by emphasis and said: ﴿that Allah﴾ [that is], by His majesty and the might of His perfection, ﴿causes to enter﴾, that is, He causes to enter in an entry about which there is no doubt, ﴿the night into the day﴾, so that it disappears within it such that nothing of it is seen, and then, behold, the day has spread over the whole earth, faster than a glance. ﴿And causes to enter the day﴾, that is, He causes it to enter likewise ﴿into the night﴾, so that it is concealed until no trace of it remains, and then, behold, the night has covered the horizons, their easts and their wests, in the span of a moment. He, glorified is He, then distinguishes each of the two from the other after its vanishing, and this is one of the meanings. So likewise the creation and the resurrection are within His power, by His might and wisdom, for reaching His hearing and the penetration of His sight. Since this is a meaning that renews itself in every day and night, He expressed it in the present tense.

Since the two luminaries are two great bodies that have been directed along a known course with a measure that does not vary, He expressed concerning them in the past tense immediately after what they are signs of, and said: ﴿And He subjected the sun﴾ as a sign for the day through the entry of the night into it, ﴿and the moon﴾ as a sign for the night likewise! Then He resumed what they were subjected to, and said: ﴿each﴾, that is, of them, ﴿runs﴾, that is, in its orbit, proceeding, continuing, reaching, and ending.

Since the focal point of the surah's purpose is wisdom, and this world is tied to the wisdom of causes and the gradual process, and the extension in origination and direction, the place was suited to the particle of limit, so He said: ﴿for a term appointed﴾, which it does not exceed, in known stations throughout the whole orbit, neither increasing nor decreasing; this one completes it in a month [once], and that one in a year once; neither of them can exceed its limit, nor diminish its cycle, nor change its course.

Since there became evident through this firm arrangement, in this greatest matter, the comprehensiveness of His knowledge and the completeness of His power, He joined to "that Allah" His saying, emphasizing it because their deeds are the deeds of one who denies His knowledge of them: ﴿And that Allah﴾, that is, with what He has of the attributes of perfection mentioned and other than them. He placed the prepositional phrase first, indicating the completeness of His knowledge of deeds, as the indication has passed more than once. He generalized the address as a clarification of what preceded it, and as encouragement and warning, and said: ﴿of what you do﴾, that is, at every time, in a continuous manner, ﴿is All-Aware﴾, nothing overcomes Him, nor is anything hidden from Him, because He is the Creator of all of it, in its smallest and greatest. The servant has in its bringing into existence nothing but acquisition, because he does not know the measure of the movements and stillnesses in any part of it. Had he been its originator, he would have known it, since one whose knowledge is deficient cannot at all have the power of origination. How many times has He, glorified is He, informed in His books and through the tongues of His prophets of future matters concerning the servants, and what He said came to pass as He said, and none of them [could] oppose anything of what He said; thus His words were fulfilled, and His indications and expressions were true. This is another proof of the completeness of power over resurrection and other than it, given that the creatures across the whole earth exceed enumeration, and each of them does not cease at every moment from an action of movement and stillness, and He, glorified is He, is the originator of all of that at every instant, continuously, as long as the two alternations succeed one another and time remains, no matter of His preoccupies Him from another. The Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, when they were addressed with this, had the utmost knowledge of it, because of what he mentioned of its proof, and because of what they witnessed of the Prophet ﷺ informing about unseen matters concerning people absent and people present, some very distant, some intermediate, some near, and other states that necessitate certainty for them about this. This is their knowledge; so how could the one specifically addressed in this verse, the Prophet ﷺ, be ignorant of it, given what he witnesses of the traces of His glory, exalted is He, and what he perceives of His origination in the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and other than that of what He, glorified and exalted is He, has made him aware of from the realm of the unseen and the witnessed?

When these attributes of excellence and lofty acts were established, that there is in reality no originator except God, He said: ﴿That﴾, i.e., the mention of what He has of awesome acts and dazzling attributes, ﴿because﴾ [i.e., by reason of the fact that] ﴿God﴾ [i.e., the One than whom there is no greater], ﴿He is﴾ alone ﴿the Truth﴾, i.e., the One who is established in reality. The existence of anything else in actuality is non-existence, because it is derived from another and does not have existence from its own essence. From this is ﴿what they associate [with Him]﴾. For this reason He singled Him out by the text, saying, diverting the address (p-203) from the past tense to the third person according to the reading of the Basrans, Hamzah, and Hafs from ʿAsim, indicating anger. The reading of the rest follows the past-tense style. ﴿And that what they call upon﴾, i.e., these people whose faculties have been sealed, and he indicated the lowliness of their rank by his saying: ﴿besides Him﴾.

Since the many proofs of the falsehood of their gods had already been presented in a way that admits no addition, such as His saying ﴿This is the creation of God, so show me what those besides Him have created﴾ [Luqman: 11], and since He here increased the use of the Divine Name in place of the pronoun to draw attention to the great station, no need arose for emphasis with the separating pronoun (ḍamīr al-faṣl, the pronoun of separation). So He said: ﴿the falsehood﴾, i.e., truly non-existence, which does not deserve to be ascribed divinity in any way. Otherwise it would have been unable to prevent any of these acts even once. When these acts exist in this order, it is known that He is the One who has no equal.

Since they were raising these [false gods] above their ranks and magnifying them without right, He said: ﴿And that God﴾, i.e., the Supreme King alone. Since the two luminaries (al-nayyirān, the sun and the moon) were among those worshipped besides God, and since both combine loftiness and greatness, while in their own essence they have nothing but non-existence, let alone lowliness and smallness, He concluded with His saying: ﴿He is the Most High, the Great﴾, i.e., exalted beyond having any opposite contend with Him in His loftiness, or any rival match Him in His greatness.

(p. 204) When the verse contained three things, he followed it with its proof, saying, as a reminder that our sailing in the ship is like the sailing of the stars in their orbit, and that the passage of our lives through the orbit of days, until it carries us into the sea of death, is like the passage of each of night and day through the orbit of the sun, until it carries one into the other, so that it departs as though it had never been. This would not be sound without His being the sole possessor of truth, exaltedness and greatness. It is specific to the address of the highest of people, as a reminder that, because these things are so familiar, they have turned people away from reflecting on them. Thus, in reality, the verse [urges] reflection upon them. This is confirmed by the turn to address everyone when giving the reason: ﴿Do you not see that the ships﴾, meaning the vessels, large and small, ﴿sail﴾, meaning carrying you, bearing what you cannot transport by land of the like of it, ﴿through the sea﴾. He expressed the relation by the adverbial of place, indicating that the ship has in itself nothing but sinking [in the water], because of its density and the lightness of water. So He said ﴿in the sea﴾, [meaning] on the surface of the water. [He expressed the act by its effect, because that is more loving, and so He said]: ﴿by the favor of Allah﴾, meaning by the mercy of the supreme King, who encompasses everything in knowledge and power, and by His beneficence, renewing this for you across time, in that He taught you its making, until it was readied through the hands of your father Noah, the grateful servant, upon him be peace. ﴿That He may show you of His signs﴾, meaning the wonders of His power and His proofs, [which] indicate to you that He is the Truth whose necessary existence establishes what you see of heavy loads on the surface of the water, in which a needle sinks and whatever is less than it. These [loads] are equal to other things in that all of them are from dust, so nothing distinguishes between them except Him, by the completeness of His power and His deliberate act.

Since this is a matter which, when considered in isolation from its having become familiar, dazzles the minds and bewilders the understandings, He pointed to it with His words, emphasizing it as a reminder of the heedlessness in which they are, turning the address after the plural to the singular, as a reminder of the subtlety of the matter, and that it, although it is thought to be evident, is not truly understood by anyone other than him (ﷺ): ﴿Indeed in that﴾, meaning in this awesome, marvelous, sublime matter, ﴿are signs﴾, meaning clear indications of what He possesses of attributes of perfection, in the fact that it does not sink, in its sailing to vast lands and distant regions, in the fact that its sailing is going and returning, at times with two winds and at other times with a single wind, in the rescue of your father Noah, upon him be peace, and whoever Allah willed of His creatures [with him], and the drowning of others, all the people of the earth, and in other of His affairs, matters and arts, His blessings and His trials. Even if most of this has become familiar to you, so that you have failed to recognize that it is among the extraordinary customs and the breaking of regular patterns. It is known from the conclusion of the verse before it that the intended meaning, by His words comprehending all of faith, which is two halves, a half patience and a half gratitude, and that is the completeness of the attribute of the believer, showing the place of "for you" or "for you all", is that it conveys the ruling for every one who shares with him (ﷺ) in the two described attributes: ﴿for every patient one﴾, who persists in reflecting on these blessings and recalling them in hardship and ease, and that they are from Allah, and that none other than Him has power over them, and submits to Him in all of that, preserving what reason indicates of the covenant to be grateful, and not diverting the right to other than its people, for that would entail wronging the benefactor. ﴿Grateful﴾ for it, ﴿exceedingly﴾ in each of patience and gratitude. It is known from the intensive form in each of them that one does not recognize in ease the greatness of Allah as one recognized it in hardship, except those whom Allah has disposed to that, enabled, and helped in it, by keeping the covenant and abstaining from breaking it, in accordance with what the original sound nature calls for. And few are they. [And] al-Razi said in al-Lawami': Whatever the case, patience is steadfastness in the stations of servanthood, and gratitude is seeing the blessing as coming from the true Benefactor and directing His blessings to what He loves.

(p-207) Since they were hastening toward disbelief after separating from this great sign, and after this immense blessing had been bestowed upon them, which had made them know what the preceding verse contained of His sole truth, His exaltedness and greatness, and the falsehood of their partners, He turned away from addressing them (p-207), because they had not returned after the clarity, as an indication that they deserved severe anger and punishment. So He said, expressing wonder and linking to what is implied: "As for one who is not patient and grateful, they do not see the signs in it [in the state of] their ease," ﴿And when a wave covers them﴾, meaning it rose over them while they were in it, until it became like a covering over them, because it prevented their sight from extending as it had been. ﴿A wave﴾, meaning this kind, and perhaps He used the singular because, owing to its intense turbulence and its coming one after another in succession, with some riding over others, it seems like one thing, and its origin is from motion and crowding. ﴿Like shadows﴾, [meaning] to the extent that it was like the dark mountain peaks for one standing beside them. [And to indicate their utmost submission, He repeated the greatest Name, saying]: ﴿they call upon Allah﴾, meaning, bringing to mind what a human can attain of perfection through His majesty and beauty, knowing all the content of the preceding verse of His truth, His exaltedness and greatness, and the falsehood of what they call upon besides Him, ﴿sincere to Him in religion﴾, not calling upon anything other than Him, neither with their tongues nor their hearts, because of what compelled them to that from the signs of majesty, and what forced them to it of greatness and perfection. The situation in the context of wisdom required the omission of what they called upon, to magnify the matter [therein], because of what it entailed of hardships, so that the soul might go in every direction.

Since killing by the sword was easier for them than being said of them that they [p-208] acknowledged something they denied, out of fear of the disgrace and shame of that, to the extent that one who said: "Had it not been that it would be said that I only submitted out of fear of death, and that my sons after me would be reviled for it, I would have submitted," He, glory be to Him, showed them that they had fallen, by what they did at the fear of drowning, into that, and more wondrous than it was their return to disbelief upon deliverance, because with it there was ungratefulness for the favor, which is among the greatest of foul deeds in their estimation. So He said, using the particle fa' (then) to indicate the proximity of their absurdity, their levity and their ignorance: ﴿So when He delivered them﴾, meaning He rescued them, raising them up, a great deliverance for them, gradually, from those terrors ﴿to the land﴾. They descended from that station in which they had made religion sincere, and abandoned the path of the corrupt, and they divided into two groups. ﴿Among them﴾, meaning, this is a consequence of the blessing of deliverance and is linked to it, indicating that what effected this division is only the compulsion to sincerity at sea, and their deliverance from it, [is that] among them there was ﴿one who is moderate﴾, one who exerts himself to be in the middle and inclines to remain upon the straight path, which is sincerity in monotheism, to which the compulsion had driven him. And they were few, as indicated by the explicit mention of partitive [min, "among"]. ﴿And among them is one who denies﴾ the blessing, rejecting the bridle of life in declaring this, [p-209] and he is the majority, as the indication to it has passed, and as the omission of explicit partitive [min] in it indicates. ﴿And none deny Our signs except every treacherous ingrate﴾. "Only" every patient and grateful one is moderate, either in state or in wealth. ﴿And none deny﴾, and He frightened the denier by the aspect of greatness which by nature entails retribution, so He said, turning the speech toward it: ﴿Our signs﴾, meaning he denies them despite their greatness, especially after acknowledging them. ﴿Except every treacherous﴾, meaning, extremely treacherous, great in it, because he broke the covenant, which reason guides to and fear calls to. ﴿Ungrateful﴾, meaning, greatly ungrateful for the favor of One who is continually surrounding him with His blessings, in his secret and open, in his movements and stillness, and there is no blessing except that it is from Him. Hence came the intensification in the two attributes, and it is known that they are antithesis (tibaq) and correspondence (muqabalah) to the conclusion of the preceding one, and that the verse is of ihtibak (a device in which each part omits what is mentioned in the other): the mention of the moderate first indicates "and among them is one who denies" second, and the restriction of denial to the ungrateful second indicates the restriction of moderation to the grateful first.

Al-Baghawi said: It was said: it was revealed concerning Ikrimah ibn Abi Jahl, when he fled, may Allah be pleased with him, to the sea in the year of the Conquest, and a violent wind came upon them, meaning: the passengers said, as was their custom: "Make [religion] sincere, for your gods will avail you nothing here." Ikrimah, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "If Allah rescues me from this, I will surely return to Muhammad and surely place my hand in his," and the wind calmed. So Ikrimah, may Allah be pleased with him, returned to Makkah, embraced Islam, and his Islam was excellent. Mujahid said: "moderate in speech [concealing disbelief]," and al-Kalbi said: "moderate in speech," meaning among the disbelievers, because some of them were more extreme in speech and higher in fabrication than others.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 31, verse 33:

When the subtleties of wisdom (*hikmah*) had become manifest through what was mentioned in this surah, and the banners of greatness and the effectiveness of the Word had spread throughout the two horizons, and the tongues of power had made clear the proofs of God's oneness, leaving no room for any foreign tongue to claim otherwise, it became as evident as the sun that there must be a return to the Day of Judgment (*yawm al-fasl*). He concluded with the denier. Glorified is He, He commanded His servants in general, both the disobedient and the obedient, to turn toward Him, and He warned them of what they would come to. He addressed them by their lowest attributes, because of the instability (*dhabdhabah*) they had, as the state explained just before had made known. So He said:

﴿O mankind﴾, that is, all of them. He turned the speech to the attribute that reminds of beneficence, as encouragement and warning, and said: ﴿Fear your Lord﴾, that is, the One besides whom there is no god [for you], because there is no benefactor to you other than Him. Let this be a fear that lasts, while you are striving to the utmost in it, not as you did when you saw the terrors of the sea.

Since the sovereignty of the one God, the King [*al-Ilah al-Malik*], necessitates fear of Him, because there is no equal to Him, and since it is known of Him that He does not review His servants to repay them for their deeds without fear, as one fears when one knows that He will review them, He said: ﴿And fear a Day﴾ which resembles no other days, and against whose least terror the terror of the sea and anything else is not counted as anything at all.

When a guilty person knows that he has someone with the King who will ward off [punishment] from him, his fear slackens. The affection, compassion, tenderness and mercy between parent and child, which call one to protect, help, and sacrifice oneself and one's wealth, are greater than what exists between others. So when the one of them cannot avail the other, then the rest are negated all the more. He said: ﴿nor does a parent avail [*la yajzi*] (lit. "compensate for" or "suffice") ...﴾, that is, does not suffice in it. Perhaps he omitted the complement to indicate that this is their state always. However, He, glorified is He, placed in this abode causes by which He veiled His power, so the ignorant one attributes the matter to them and ascribes it to them. But there, the causes vanish, the clouds of doubt are dispelled, and the exclusive greatness of the Lord of lords becomes manifest.

Since the compassion of a parent, despite encompassing all the days of his life, is greatest [so that he prefers his child's life over his own and prefers to bear pains and wealth himself], He began with it, saying: ﴿a parent﴾, whoever he may be, ﴿for his child﴾ [i.e.,] no kind of recompense is produced from him or renewed at any time, even if it is certain that the child is his. The use of the imperfect [*al-mudari'*] indicates that the parent is still moved by parenthood to compassion for the child, and his affection and tenderness are continually renewed. The object is either omitted, because that is stronger and more emphatic in negation, or it is indicated by what is in the second clause that follows.

Since a child is not expected to avail his parent in calamities until he reaches maturity, He postponed mention of it in an expression indicating the permanence of the general negation, and said: ﴿nor is a child [*mawlud*] (any child whatsoever) one who will compensate for his parent﴾ [*jazin 'an walidihi*, active participle form], ﴿anything﴾ of recompense, even if it is known that he is part of him. In the use of ﴿huwa﴾ ("he") there is an indication that what is negated is his benefit by himself, so there is a hope that God may permit him to benefit [the parent] when the condition is met. He expressed it here with the active participle [*ism al-fa'il*] because it is the child's nature that this should be a constant habit toward his father, given the rights the father has over him. The verb is applied to one who is not characterized by the root meaning of its derivation, so He used it for the father, because the child has no right over him that requires him to constantly ward off [punishment] from him, and that is not part of his nature or something he is characterized by, so he is not free of it. This is like a king who sews: it is correct to say in that situation that "he sews," but it is not correct to call him "a tailor," because that is not his craft or his nature.

Since it is known that the tongue of their state says: "Is this Day really going to happen?" this question was answered by His saying, emphasizing it because of the place of their denial, and turning the speech to the Greatest Name [*al-ism al-a'zam*] because fulfilling promises requires it: ﴿Indeed, the promise of God﴾, to whom belong all the foundations of might and majesty, ﴿is true﴾. That is, He, glorified is He, has promised it with the majesty of His majesty and the greatness of His power and perfection. How, then, could it be permitted to enter into a thought, let alone your thoughts, that He would break it, when [even] the lowest of you, O Arabs, all of you, would not consider breaking his promise, even if he incurred dangers in doing so and endured great hardships? When His affair was established, and their love for the prison of this visible existence was making them forget that Day, because of what He, glorified is He, placed in this existence of pleasures, its consequence was His saying, emphasizing the gravity of the matter: ﴿So let not the life of this world deceive you﴾, that is, with its adornments, and [not] what delights one who has no reflection of its fading splendor. He repeated the verb and the emphasis to indicate that their familiarity with the present covers over them the falsehood and the manifest deception and delusion within it. So He said, using the explicit noun rather than a pronoun for the sake of increasing warning and caution: ﴿And let not the Deceiver deceive you concerning God﴾, the One than whom there is nothing greater and no equal to Him, even with His guardianship over you, ﴿the Deceiver﴾ [i.e.,] the one of great deception, the most extreme in it. This is Satan, than whom there is nothing more contemptible, because of what he has gathered of distance, expulsion, and burning, together with his enmity, by adorning for you its affairs, diverting you by magnifying its worth, making you forget its treachery and deceit, its toil and evil, its harm and injury. This leads you to turn away from that Day, so you do not prepare for it as a return, and you do not take provision for it, because of the forbearance and respite of God that accompany his deception.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Heedlessness [*al-ghirrah*] is that one commits sin and hopes for forgiveness."

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 31, verse 34:

Since it is evident that the tongue of their state, after the question about the realization of that Day (they ask about its time, as has passed in more than one verse and will come at the end of the verse after it), whether out of obstinacy and mockery or in earnest, He answered that question by adding to it its counterparts from the keys of the unseen (*mafatih al-ghayb*, the five keys of the unseen) mentioned in the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, which follows. This is because of the wisdom for which the surah was revealed. He arranged them from the most distant to the nearest from the knowledge of creation. He said, emphasizing what they believe about their soothsayers and making the Greatest Name explicit rather than using a pronoun, because the context strongly demands it: ﴿Indeed, Allah﴾, that is, with all His majesty and all the attributes of perfection, ﴿with Him﴾, that is, exclusively. Had it been said simply "*'indahu*" without more, it would not convey presence. Had it been said "*ladayhi*," the use of "*ladā*," which denotes presence, would have implied that this is a metaphor for its very nearness, and would have implied that His knowledge varies in its connection to things in particularity or generality, because "*ladā*" is more specific than "*'inda*." So "*'inda*" was more suitable to the intended meaning, for it conveys having full capacity for knowledge while allowing for the possibility of its delay, and it is free from any corrupt possibility entering it. ﴿is the knowledge of the Hour﴾, that is, the time of its establishment, and there is no knowledge of it at all for anyone other than Him.

Since He, glorified is He, had set signs for it that produce conjectures about its nearness, and had revealed some of its matters, He expressed it with "knowledge." Since they had persistently asked about its time, and since it was the most remote of the five from the knowledge of creation, and since it was one single thing that cannot be divided, ﴿it is but a single blast﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 13] ﴿and behold, they are on the surface of the earth﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 14], He presented it in a nominal sentence that indicates permanence and stability, in the manner of restriction. This is the first key of the keys of the unseen, by which open up knowledge that is too vast to be confined: the souls' standing in their bodies, inclining toward their tastes with all their members, their forms, colors, and all their conditions; the flying of spirits at the blowing into them and their enclosure in them, with the variety of their kinds, the difference of their shapes and heights, the diversity of their tongues and deeds, and other matters and wonders of what is decreed. Then their striving to the place of standing, then their standing, then their reckoning, until the two groups settle in the two abodes. Along with this is their surging in the intense crowding and great distress, some pressing on others, seeking one who will intercede for them in the reckoning, until the Chosen One (ﷺ) stands in the praised station, which the first and last will envy him for, until the heavens are split and their stars are dimmed, and the angels descend after rising from their sleep, of whom no inhabitant of any heaven can count the multitude. How much more so, when the heaven has creaked and has rightly been entitled to creak, with no place in it the size of a foot without an angel standing in prayer. Along with this is the changing of the earth, the vanishing of the mountains, the leveling of buildings, hills and dunes, and other things that none knows in their true knowledge except Him, glorified is He.

The second key: the sign of Allah in His creation concerning the establishment of the Hour, and the strongest of the proofs for it, which is the sending down of rain. It reveals the mixing that lies deep in the earth with the soil that was once vegetation, and its return to vegetation as it was before, with the variety of its colors, measures, forms, branches and sprigs, scents and tastes, benefits and natures, and other of its states and kinds, which none can encompass in knowledge except its Creator, Originator and Maker.

Since they attributed rainfall to the stars (*al-anwa'*), He ascribed the sending down to Himself, glorified is He, to convey favor. He used the verbal sentence to indicate renewal, and said: ﴿and He sends down the rain﴾, with the particle of totality (*lam al-istighraq*) that takes the place of encompassing with "*kull*" (every). This indicates exclusivity in knowing its time, place, measure and other of its matters, for whoever truly does something, no one knows the time of its doing before it occurs except from Him.

The third key: knowledge of wombs, which is the second level in indicating resurrection, revealing their shaping, formation, configuration and measure, in terms of male and female, with clarity or obscurity, unity or multiplicity, completeness or deficiency, and what lies therein of differences in measures, natures, characters and dispositions, earnings and crafts, and changes in the length of life and sustenance in times and places, and other conditions that none can count except the Creator of souls and the Reviver of bones. Since creatures have conjectures about these matters, because of the many circumstances and treatments, about the existence of the pregnancy first, then whether it is male or female second, and similar matters, by the signs that have been set for them, arising from long experience and frequent practice, He expressed it with knowledge and said: ﴿and He knows what is in the wombs﴾, whether male or female, living or dead, and otherwise. The present tense is used to indicate the renewal of the foetuses moment by moment. The discussion of the particle of exclusivity and exclusivity of knowledge is the same as in the previous one.

The fourth key: the earning that arises from what is in the wombs, which opens the treasures of happiness and the calamities of wretchedness, and which reveals the realities of hearts in their truthfulness at trial and their falsehood, the measures of resolves and the ranks of natural dispositions, and the states of people at that time in friendship and enmity, intelligence and dullness, clarity and turbidity, safety and cunning, and other matters of health and sickness, amid differing affairs and wonders of what is decreed, in good and evil, none can encompass except its Originator, who implanted it in His servants and deposited it in them. Since a human being, though it is the thing closest to him and most inseparable from him, does not know it despite the abundance of means to know it, He expressed it with *dirayah* (cognizance, acquired knowledge), because it indicates the means by way of turning the mind and circulating opinion, as was mentioned in Surah Yusuf (peace be upon him), that the root *d-r-y* revolves around turning, and among its necessities is the employment of stratagem and deep reflection. Thus it is more specific than general knowledge. So He said: ﴿and no soul knows﴾, that is, among human souls and others, ﴿what it will earn tomorrow﴾, that is, in the future, of good or evil, in any way whatsoever. He emphasized the meaning with "*dhā*" (what) and the stripping of the verb, and said: ﴿what it will earn tomorrow﴾. The negation of the servant's knowledge of this, despite its being the thing closest to him, is clear evidence of the negation of knowing what is before it, because that is more hidden than it. The affirmation of His knowledge of it, glorified and exalted is He, has already passed. So this takes the form of restriction. It is also known that the earning cannot be ascribed to the servant in the absolute sense, because if it were created by him he would know it with certainty. Thus it is established that He, glorified and exalted is He, is its Creator, and so His exclusivity in knowing it is known from this aspect as well.

The fifth key: the place of death, which is the conclusion of the worldly matter and the folding up of the record of visible effects, and the beginning of the otherworldly matter that manifests the states of the barzakh (intermediate realm), in descending with those awaiting the rest of the journey to the circle of resurrection, and the state of gathering, to what is there of gain and loss, honor and humiliation, and what the spirit has of connection with the body, and its rank in height and depth, ascent and descent, and beyond that, to what has no end, of which none knows the details, totalities, universals and particulars except its Inventor, its Creator and its Maker.

Since a human being cannot know it by any kind of stratagem, out of his intense caution regarding it [and his love], even if he spent all he possesses in order to know it, He expressed it differently from the previous one, and said, emphasizing by repeating the negation and the predicate: ﴿and no soul knows﴾, and He made it explicit, because it is clearer and more fitting for generality, and said: ﴿in what land it will die﴾. He did not say "at what time," because one cannot escape time, while one can escape a specific place, and because everyone's aversion to death is known. So this was the strongest evidence of his ignorance of the place of his death, for had he known it he would have distanced himself from it and not approached it.

Al-Bukhari narrated the hadith of the keys from Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The keys of the unseen are five, none knows them except Allah." Then he recited: ﴿Indeed Allah has with Him the knowledge of the Hour﴾, to the end of the verse. He also narrated from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, in the hadith of Jibril (peace be upon him) asking the Prophet (ﷺ) about the signs of the Hour, and he informed him of some of them and said: "Five things none knows except Allah: ﴿Indeed Allah has with Him the knowledge of the Hour, and He sends down the rain﴾," to the end of the surah. The hadith thus clearly indicates that the verse concerns what Allah, glorified and exalted is He, alone knows. He arranged them in this order for the wisdom that has preceded, and knew the secret of mentioning them sometimes in a nominal sentence, sometimes in a verbal one, sometimes without any mention of knowledge, sometimes with mention of it, ascribed to Him, glorified is He, but not in the manner of restriction, and sometimes by negating knowledge from anyone else only, without ascribing the verb to Him. And the secret of His saying "in what land," rather than "at what time," is known, as in some [transmissions] of the hadith.

Since He, glorified is He, had established for Himself the exclusivity of knowledge of these things against creation, He then affirmed what is more comprehensive, so that it is included implicitly, and He thus informs of His knowledge of them twice. He said, with emphasis, because they deny some of what He informs of, and that entails their denial of some of His knowledge: ﴿Indeed Allah﴾, that is, the one characterized by perfection, greatness, magnificence and majesty, ﴿is All-Knowing﴾, that is, of all-encompassing knowledge of all matters, universals and particulars. So He affirmed absolute knowledge for Himself, glorified is He, after negating it from others in these five, sometimes explicitly and sometimes by way of priority or by necessary implication. Thus the proof corresponds to the claim. And Allah is the Granter of success.

Having affirmed knowledge in this manner, He emphasized it for the sake of what the surah was revealed for, with His saying: ﴿All-Aware﴾, that is, He knows the hidden affairs and concealed contents of hearts, just as He knows their outward aspects and manifest forms; all are equal before Him. He is the All-Wise in His essence and attributes, and for this reason He concealed these keys from His servants, because had He made them aware of them, much wisdom would have been lost, given the variation of this order and its firm arrangement. Thus the end of the surah corresponds to its beginning, which informed of the wisdom of His attribute by affirming wisdom together with affirming knowledge and awareness, along with establishing the matter of the Hour, which is the key to the abode of the Hereafter. Whoever knows this attribute as it truly should be known, and takes on the character to which it calls and urges, especially certainty in the Hereafter, becomes wise, aware, knowing, refined, guided, brought near, and exalted. Glorified is He whose speech this is, exalted is His magnificence, and mighty is His aim. There is no god but Him, and He is the Subtle.
